questions.prompt: What does an LLM do at each step while it writes an answer?
options: Looks up the finished answer in a database and copies it out
Scores every possible next token, picks one and adds it to the text
Writes the whole answer at once, then checks it word by word
Asks a person to choose the next word from a short list
questions.explanation: An LLM reads the text so far, gives every token in its vocabulary a probability of coming next, picks one, adds it and repeats until it picks an "end" token or reaches a length limit.

options: The list of topics it is allowed to talk about
The words it has learnt to spell correctly
The languages it can translate between
The full list of tokens it can choose from at each step
questions.explanation: The vocabulary is every token the model knows. At each step it gives all of them a probability. GPT-2's vocabulary had 50,257 tokens.

questions.prompt: After "Dal, chawal aur", a model gives "sabzi" a probability of 35%. What does that mean?
options: The model thinks sabzi has a 35% chance of being the next word
35% of people in the training data ate sabzi for lunch
The model is 35% sure that sabzi is a real word
Sabzi will appear in 35% of the words in the answer
questions.explanation: A probability is the model's score for how likely that token is to come next. With sampling, "sabzi" would be picked about 35 times in 100.

questions.prompt: A developer makes a model always pick the single most likely next token. What are they most likely to notice in long answers?
options: The answers become wildly creative and unpredictable
The model stops after the first word every time
The text gets flat and the model starts repeating itself
The model refuses to answer questions about facts
questions.explanation: Always taking the top choice is called greedy picking. It sounds safe, but long text comes out flat, and models that do it often get stuck repeating themselves. Sampling fixes this.

questions.prompt: You're building a tool that converts recipes from cups to grams, and you want the same answer every time. Which temperature suits it best?
options: A high temperature, so the answers stay fresh and varied
A low temperature, close to 0, so it nearly always picks the top token
Any temperature, because it only affects how fast the model writes
A temperature of exactly 2, the highest OpenAI allows
questions.explanation: A low temperature makes the most likely tokens even more likely, so answers are focused and predictable. That's what you want for facts, maths and conversions.

questions.prompt: You want a model to brainstorm 20 unusual names for a chai stall. What does raising the temperature do?
options: Gives less likely words more of a chance, so the names vary more
Makes the model check each name on the internet first
Makes the model write faster, so it can fit in more names
Makes the model choose only names it saw in its training text
questions.explanation: A higher temperature evens out the probabilities, so unusual tokens get picked more often. That's useful for brainstorming. Push it too far, though, and the names turn into nonsense.

questions.prompt: You ask a chatbot the same question twice and get two different answers. What's the most likely reason?
options: The chatbot learnt something new between your two questions
Someone at the company edited the first answer
The first answer was wrong, so the chatbot corrected itself
It picks each token by weighted chance, so different picks lead to a different answer
questions.explanation: Chatbots usually sample: each token is picked at random, weighted by its probability. Two runs make different picks, and each pick changes what comes after it.

questions.prompt: Why can't an LLM go back and fix a word it wrote earlier in the same answer?
options: Its memory is too small to hold more than one sentence
Each token it writes becomes part of the text it continues from
It is only allowed to use each word once per answer
The chat app deletes the earlier words as it goes
questions.explanation: The model only ever adds the next token to the end. Once a token is written, every later pick builds on it, so an early slip can lead the rest of the answer astray.
